title: A Long Love Song to God's Word
overview: In the Bible's longest chapter, a person under pressure keeps returning to God's teaching as their guide, comfort and hope.

parts.label: Happy are those who follow (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: The poem is built on the Hebrew alphabet: 22 sections of eight verses, and every verse in a section begins with the same letter. The word often translated "law" (Hebrew torah) means teaching or instruction, so the writer is celebrating God's guidance for life, not just a list of rules.

parts.label: Keeping the word close (vv. 9-48)
parts.note: The writer asks to be taught and wants God's words stored in the heart, likely meaning memorized and taken to heart, so they shape choices from the inside. Feeling like a temporary outsider passing through the world (v. 19), they treat this teaching as their map and even their freedom (v. 45).

parts.label: Mocked, trapped and worn out (vv. 49-88)
parts.note: Proud people mock, lie about and try to trap the writer, who asks how long the wait will be and when God will step in (vv. 82, 84), yet also says hard times stopped them drifting (vv. 67, 71). Comparing themselves to a wineskin hung in smoke (v. 83) probably pictures a leather bottle near the fire that dried out, blackened and shriveled.

parts.label: A word that stands firm (vv. 89-112)
parts.note: The writer compares God's word to the steady order of heaven and earth, something that holds when everything else has limits (v. 96). Calling it a lamp for the feet (v. 105) brings to mind a small oil lamp that lit only the next few steps on a dark path.

parts.label: Longing for God to act (vv. 113-160)
parts.note: The writer swings between trust and pleading, calling God a safe hiding place and a shield (v. 114) while urging that it is time for the LORD to act (v. 126). They weep and are worn out with zeal because others ignore God's teaching (vv. 136, 139), an honest mix of devotion and frustration.

parts.label: Ending as a lost sheep (vv. 161-176)
parts.note: After 175 verses of commitment, the psalm ends by admitting the writer has wandered off like a lost sheep and asking God to come looking. Christians have often heard an echo of this in Jesus' story of the shepherd who searches for one lost sheep.

disagreement: Christians differ on what "your law" means for them today: some read it mainly as the commands given through Moses, part of which they see as still binding, while others read it more broadly as God's whole word or will, seen through Jesus.
think: When life feels unsteady, what do you find yourself returning to for guidance, and what makes it feel trustworthy to you?
